sections.heading: Early Life
sections.content: Ada Lovelace was born on December 10, 1815 in London.

sections.heading: Analytical Engine Notes
sections.content: In 1843, she published notes on Charles Babbage's Analytical Engine, including an algorithm often described as the first computer program.

sections.heading: Birth and Education
sections.content: Alan Turing was born on June 23, 1912 and later studied at King's College, Cambridge.

sections.heading: Wartime Work
sections.content: From 1939 to 1945, Turing worked at Bletchley Park on codebreaking, contributing to the defeat of Nazi Germany.

sections.heading: Start at NACA/NASA
sections.content: Katherine Johnson joined the NACA West Area Computing unit in 1953, and later became a key mathematician at NASA.

sections.heading: Apollo Era
sections.content: In 1969, her trajectory calculations supported the success of Apollo 11.

sections.heading: Military Service
sections.content: Grace Hopper joined the U.S. Naval Reserve in 1943 and worked on the Harvard Mark I computer.

sections.heading: Compiler Contributions
sections.content: In 1952, Hopper's team created the A-0 system, one of the earliest compilers.

sections.heading: Proposal of the Web
sections.content: In March 1989, Tim Berners-Lee proposed an information management system at CERN that became the World Wide Web.

sections.heading: First Website
sections.content: The first website went live in 1991, explaining what the web was and how to use it.

sections.heading: Frequency-Hopping Patent
sections.content: In 1941, Hedy Lamarr and George Antheil filed a patent for a frequency-hopping communication system.

sections.heading: Recognition
sections.content: Lamarr received broader recognition for her technical contribution decades later, including an award in 1997.
